list.listitem: Extrahepatic obstruction accounts for 40% of adult patients who present with jaundice as the primary symptom and 20% of those with new-onset jaundice. B

Ultrasound of the abdomen is the most appropriate initial study to evaluate patients presenting with jaundice when the clinical scenario and laboratory examination make extrahepatic obstruction unlikely. B

CT of the abdomen is the most appropriate initial study to evaluate patients presenting with jaundice and acute abdominal pain if there is fever, known chlolelithiasis, or history of biliary surgery. B

Ultrasound or CT of the abdomen are indicated for otherwise healthy patients with painless jaundice and one of the following red flags: weight loss, fatigue, anorexia, or duration of symptoms greater than 3 months. B
If there is no sign of extrahepatic obstruction after imaging and laboratory analysis, evaluate patients for intrahepatic and hepatocellular causes of jaundice. C

background.definition: Jaundice is the yellow-orange discoloration of the skin, bulbar conjunctiva, and mucous membranes that results from the elevated concentration of bilirubin in plasma.

list.listitem: A study of 732 adult outpatients and inpatients with new-onset jaundice (total serum bilirubin of >3 mg/dL) found that 72% had conjugated hepatocellular disease/damage or intrahepatic cholestasis (direct predominant); 20% conjugated extrahepatic obstruction (direct predominant); and 8% unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (indirect predominant).
Conjugated extrahepatic obstruction (direct predominant): 14% gallstone disease; 6.2% malignancy.

Conjugated hepatocellular disease/damage or intrahepatic cholestasis (direct predominant): 22% sepsis/altered hemodynamic states; 20.5% decompensation of pre-existing chronic liver disease; 16% alcoholic hepatitis; 8.8% acute viral hepatitis; 4% drug-induced liver injury (can be direct or indirect); 0.3% acute autoimmune hepatitis.
Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (indirect predominant): 5.6% Gilberts disease; 2.5% hemolysis.
Other studies indicate that extrahepatic obstruction accounts for 40% of adult patients who present with jaundice as the primary symptom.

Bilirubin, the end product of heme degradation, binds tightly to albumin in the serum and is transported to the liver for conversion to conjugated (direct) bilirubin from unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin.
Conjugated bilirubin is then secreted across the canicular membranes. Once bile is released into enterohepatic circulation, it is predominately reabsorbed in the terminal ileum.
Urobilinogen is formed in the colon and partially reabsorbed after deconjugation of bile by gut flora.
Disorders that cause increased bilirubin production, decreased hepatic bilirubin clearance, and hereditary defects in bilirubin conjugation lead to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
Disorders that cause extrahepatic or intrahepatic obstruction or hepatocellular destruction lead to predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Artificial light decreases the sensitivity of the conjunctival examination for the presence of icterus. Include in the physical examination a careful evaluation of the liver, presence or absence of other stigmata of chronic liver disease, and presence or absence of ascites.
Jaundice is rare in patients with acute cholecystitis. The presence of jaundice increases the likelihood of ascites being present in a patient with increasing abdominal girth.

For more detailed information on the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, hemolysis, and Gilbert disease; see those chapters. Neonatal jaundice is also covered in a separate chapter.

The initial approach to a patient with jaundice is to determine whether hyperbilirubinemia exists. If serum bilirubin levels are normal, consider pseudojaundice and drug reactions.

Initial laboratory tests in the patient who appears jaundiced should also include direct bilirubin, AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase (alk phos), gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT), LDH, urine analysis for bilirubin and urobilinogen, CBC, PT, and albumin. Other laboratory tests will likely be warranted as well based on history and physical examination (see ).

If hyperbilirubinemia is present, determine whether urine bilirubin or increased serum direct bilirubin is present. If there is a normal serum level of direct bilirubin (less than 15% of total bilirubin), an absence of bilirubinuria, and/or an increase in urine urobilinogen, evaluate for causes of unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia.

Consider benign genetic disorders of bilirubin metabolism in patients with a direct hyperbilirubinemia if other causes are unlikely and all other labs are normal (eg, AST, ALT, induce, alk phos, albumin, and PT).

Imaging recommendations from the American College of Radiology guidelines are listed below: Acute abdominal pain: CT recommended for patients with at least one of the following: fever, history of biliary surgery, or known cholelithiasis. Painless jaundice: ultrasound or CT of the abdomen recommended for otherwise healthy patients with one or more of the following: weight loss, fatigue, anorexia, or duration of symptoms greater than 3 months. Painless jaundice in patients who cannot tolerate a radical surgical procedure: ultrasound or CT of the abdomen or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography(ERCP)/endoscopic ultrasound is recommended in patients with one or more of the following: weight loss, fatigue, anorexia, or duration of symptoms greater than 3 months. Mechanical obstruction unlikely: ultrasound of the abdomen is recommended as the initial study. Confusing clinical picture: ultrasound or CT of the abdomen are options as the initial study.

Perform further examination of the biliary tree (eg, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, ERCP, surgical exploration) if imaging reveals dilated bile ducts or if there is a high pretest probability of extrahepatic obstruction.

Investigate for intrahepatic cholestasis or causes of hepatocellular injury if imaging studies reveal no dilatation of the bile ducts and ALT or AST are abnormal. An abnormal PT or albumin raises the possibility of significant alterations in liver synthetic function.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the evaluation of the patient with jaundice.

feature.caption: Differential Diagnoses of Jaundice.
feature.feature_body: Pseudojaundice (normal laboratory evaluation) Carotenemia Drug induced (rifabutin, novobiocin) Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (normal direct bilirubin, urine negative for bilirubin) Hereditary causes (Gilbert's disease, Crigler-Najjar syndrome) Hemolysis (eg, hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinopathies, thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, glucose 6-phosphodiesterase deficiency) Ineffective erythropoesis (eg, hemoglobinopathies, folate deficiency, iron deficiency anemia) Medications (eg, highly active antiretroviral therapy) Resorption of hematomas Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (concern for intrahepatic cholestasis or hepatocellular damage) Viral hepatitis (eg, hepatitis A, B, or C viruses, EBV, CMV, herpes simplex virus) Alcoholic hepatitis Genetic liver diseases (eg, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis, hemachromatosis, Wilson's disease, progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis syndromes) Immune/ Autoimmune (eg, autoimmune cholangiopathy, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, graft vs host disease, vanishing bile duct syndromes) Drug- or toxin-induced liver injury (acetaminophen, isoniazid, methyltestosterone) Ischemic hepatitis/ vascular compromise (eg, Budd-Chiari syndrome, heart failure, or portal vein thrombosis) Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease Mass lesions (eg, abscess, cyst, hepatocellular carcinoma, metastatic tumors) Cholestasitic syndromes Infiltrative diseases Extrahepatic cholestasis Malignancy Choledocholithiasis Primary or secondary sclerosing cholangitis Chronic pancreatitis AIDS cholangiopathy Ascending cholangitis
